body:
## Problem

- A customer on a 6-hour schedule is reported as having stopped syncing, while every scheduled sync is running on time. The only tell is the job history.
- A v3 run that extracts zero rows stamps `last_full_run_at` and deliberately leaves `last_synced_at` where it is — that field doubles as the signals watermark (`partition_field > last_synced_at`).
- `stalled_schema_queryset` reads only `last_synced_at`, so a schema whose source is simply quiet drifts past `3 x sync_frequency_interval` and qualifies.
- The sweep reports it, and `repair_stalled_schema` then rewrites a schedule that never stopped and writes `REPAIRED_SCHEMA_ERROR` on the row — a message telling the customer PostHog restarted their sync.

Zero-batch runs are the steady state for a quiet source, so this is the normal path for a whole class of schemas, not an edge case.

<!-- posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0ca81-b0be-7b69-a5c4-179393b24665 -->
## Origin

- Conversations: [ticket](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/support/tickets/01a0c9c6-8f72-0000-356e-6ba778c6ffc4)
- First signal: 2026-09-22
- Inbox report: [open](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/inbox/reports/01a0ca81-b0be-7b69-a5c4-179393b24665)
- Likely cause: [`34d4192`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/commit/34d41925241a5b5b130366f0c9762131bfc78678)
- Task started by: auto-start, after the report was rated P2 and ready to fix
<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0ca81-b0be-7b69-a5c4-179393b24665 -->

## Changes

- A schema whose recent runs found nothing to import is no longer reported as a stalled schedule, and no longer gets its schedule "repaired". One that genuinely stopped running still is.
- Silence is measured from the later of `last_synced_at` and `last_full_run_at`, so the predicate asks "when did a sync last run" rather than "when did data last change". `stalled_for` reports from the same stamp.
- `last_synced_at` is untouched, so the signals watermark keeps its meaning.

Neither stamp covers every path alone, which is why both are read:

| Run outcome | `last_synced_at` | `last_full_run_at` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run that loaded rows | advances | advances |
| v3 run that extracted zero rows | unchanged | advances |
| Fast return on a negative probe | advances | unchanged |

That union is `ExternalDataSchema.last_run_at`, so the invariant behind it sits next to the stamps. The stale-data warning from [#104604](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/104604) in `sync_status.py` now reads the property instead of its own copy.

Mechanical: the ISO parse moves onto `ExternalDataSchema.last_full_run`, shared with `_fast_return_eligible`, which applied the same unparseable-and-naive rules by hand.

- The run stamp is compared in SQL, so the sweep and the repair command keep their `LIMIT`.
- A Python filter after the `LIMIT` let quiet schemas take every slot. A Python filter before it loaded every quiet candidate on each hourly sweep.
- Only an ISO stamp with an offset is cast. Postgres raises on an unparseable string and reads a naive one in the session zone.

### Considered and rejected

Advancing `last_synced_at` on the zero-batch v3 path, so the field means what its name says. [#104604](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/104604) rejects that for the signals watermark: a row that arrives late with a `partition_field` between two quiet runs would never emit a signal. This change works with that decision instead of reverting it.

## How did you test this code?

Automated only. No sync was run and no schema was inspected in production.

`test_a_schema_whose_runs_found_nothing_to_import_is_not_stalled` reproduces the report and fails on master. It calls `limit=1` with the quiet schema sorted first, so it also fails when the limit applies before the run-stamp filter. So does `test_a_schema_whose_runs_also_stopped_is_still_stalled`, which pins that the run stamp did not become a way to never report anything, and asserts `stalled_for` measures from the newer stamp.

`test_an_unusable_run_stamp_falls_back_to_the_sync_stamp` guards the SQL cast. Without the format guard, Postgres raises on the unparseable stamp and reads the recent naive stamp as fresh, so both cases fail.

Not run: any frontend or Storybook check. Backend-only, renders no UI.

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

None. No documented behavior changes — the stall window and its threshold are the same, only the timestamp they measure from.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Fully autonomous

**Agent:** PostHog Desktop (Claude Code), Opus 5

The first implementation advanced `last_synced_at` on the zero-batch v3 path, which is what the inbox report asked for. Searching open PRs before opening this one surfaced [#104604](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/104604), which fixes the same report from the reader side and documents why that write is wrong. That commit was dropped and the work moved to the stall sweep, which #104604 does not cover: it changes the query-result warning in `products/data_warehouse/backend/sync_status.py`, while the sweep and the repair command read the predicate in `products/warehouse_sources/backend/stalled_schedules.py`. The two are complementary, and the branch was force-updated so only the shipped approach is in its history.

No duplicate: `gh pr list --state open --search "last_synced_at"` found #104604 (above) and nothing touching the stall predicate.

Public artifact: the work started from an inbox report built on support and analytics data. No customer name, account, schema, or figure from it appears in the diff or this description. The test fixtures use the repo's existing helpers with invented intervals.

Skills invoked: none available in this session beyond the repo conventions in `CLAUDE.md`; the writing rules there and in the PR template were followed directly.

A cleanup pass ran over the branch after it opened, and its second commit is the result: the stamp union moved onto `last_run_at` so the two readers stop re-deriving it, the per-row stall window got a name, and the reasoning it had stated from both sides was cut back to one place. A suggestion to reuse `ensure_utc` for the naive case was skipped — it treats a naive value as UTC by contract, and this stamp is written only by our own code as an aware timestamp, so a naive one means something unexpected wrote it. `_fast_return_eligible` already rejects it, and inventing a zone here would invent freshness.

A second session (PostHog Desktop, Claude Code, Opus 5.5) fixed the CodeRabbit comment on `limit`, then moved the run-stamp check into SQL after a `dc-review-pr` pass found the Python filter loaded every quiet candidate. Skills invoked in that session: writing-tests, writing-code-comments, writing-pr-descriptions, dc-review-pr.

CodeRabbit CLI pass: none. Neither `cr` nor `coderabbit` is installed on this machine, so the PR opens without a local pass.
